title: A Little-Known Teaching Strategy That Makes Learning Easier -learning-easier/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies a common teacher habit—warning students in advance that upcoming content is difficult—as counterproductive, arguing that labeling content as hard actually makes it hard, particularly for students who are already behind academically and who mentally check out at the first warning. He explains that this habit plants seeds of doubt that rattle student confidence and undermine learning before it even begins. His recommended fix is to teach everything with the same level of detail, attention, and enthusiasm, communicating unwavering belief in students' ability to understand it, and to go a step further by explicitly framing material as easy and doable. He cautions that this framing only works if the instruction itself is genuinely clear, detailed, and well-sequenced enough to actually be doable, and closes with an anecdote about being asked what his teaching "method" was, to which he answered simply that he tells students it's easy.
points: Telling students that content is "hard" actually makes it harder, especially for students already behind academically.
Struggling students who hear content labeled difficult often check out immediately, assuming they won't succeed.
The remedy is to teach with consistent detail and enthusiasm regardless of perceived difficulty, avoiding any hint of doubt.
Framing material as easy or doable only works if the instruction is genuinely clear, detailed, and well-sequenced.
Guiding students from one success to the next, rather than warning them of difficulty, builds transformational academic confidence.
quotes: When you tell students that something is hard, when you label it as hard, then it becomes hard. It becomes exactly what you say it is.
Sadly, students who are behind academically are the most affected. The second they hear you say that something is difficult, they check out.
Just as calling something difficult makes it difficult, calling something doable makes it doable. In other words, if you pretend it’s easy, then it becomes easy.
Now, it's important to point out that the strategy only works if your instruction is up to snuff.
One of the secrets to great teaching, and galloping progress, is to guide your students from one success to the next, all day every day.
